html: This is the fast arm of the same stress response, and the one that the noise literature measures most often. The splanchnic nerve releases acetylcholine onto the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla; the receptor it opens lets calcium in, and calcium is what couples the stimulus to the emptying of the granules. What is in those granules has been built by four enzymes in a row: tyrosine hydroxylase makes L-DOPA, which is the step that sets the pace, a decarboxylase makes dopamine, a hydroxylase makes noradrenaline, and a methyltransferase makes adrenaline. Each of those steps is visible in people who lack the enzyme, which is why the chain is drawn with enzymes rather than as a single arrow. One arc crosses from the other arm of the stress response: the glucocorticoid made by the cortex keeps the methyltransferase up, so the amount of adrenaline a chromaffin cell can release depends on what the cortex has been doing. Both catecholamines leave for the blood, and aircraft noise raises them, noradrenaline in exposed mice and adrenaline in people after a night of noise events, in proportion to how many events there were. The second half of the module follows noradrenaline to the kidney, where it binds a beta-adrenergic receptor on the cells that make renin and drives renin into the blood. Renin cuts angiotensinogen, the converting enzyme finishes the job, and the product is angiotensin II, which is the molecule the vascular module takes as its input and the one that turns on the oxidase. No noise study measures renin itself: what is measured is the angiotensin II at the end of this chain, so that is where the evidence is attached, and the renin step is drawn as mechanism rather than as a finding.
